title: Auditing evaluation artifacts and data leakage in large language model systems for rare disease diagnosis
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Auditing evaluation artifacts and data leakage in large language model systems for rare disease diagnosis
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Augmented large language model (LLM) systems have reported high benchmark accuracies in rare disease diagnosis, yet their real-world clinical utility remains unproven. A recent meta-analysis flagged augmented LLM diagnostic evaluations as having a high risk of bias due to suspected data leakage; however, the precise impact of these vulnerabilities on model inference has yet to be fully quantified. In this study, we present a comprehensive empirical audit to quantify evaluation artifacts across prevailing AI paradigms, using a repository of over 60,000 cases from diverse public and independent clinical cohorts. By reconstructing a state-of-the-art agentic framework, we demonstrate that candidate-space contamination artificially inflates performance: enforcing strict cross-dataset isolation resulted in a marked performance decline, with the cross-dataset mean Recall@1 decreasing from 54.3% (under conventional one-vs-rest evaluation) to 40.3% (Hedges' g = 0.94). Similar spatial overfitting in supervised classifiers caused diagnostic accuracy to drop from an internal mean of 42.9% to 16.7% across external cohorts (Cohen's d = 2.01). Furthermore, we quantify how LLMs infer diagnoses by exploiting retrospective therapeutic cues in clinical narratives, and how temporal misalignment in foundational knowledge bases leads to performance fluctuations. We conclude that prevailing evaluation protocols for augmented LLM systems inadvertently reflect data leakage rather than genuine medical reasoning. To address these systematic artifacts, we propose a rigorous evaluation framework - coupling strict data-isolation protocols with standardized benchmarking safeguards - to ensure future diagnostic AI for rare diseases is evaluated on actual clinical robustness.

report.summary: A large-scale audit finds that reported high accuracy for LLM-based rare disease diagnosis largely stems from data leakage and evaluation artifacts, not genuine clinical reasoning.
report.background: Roughly 300 million people worldwide live with one of 7,000+ rare diseases, and the average diagnostic odyssey stretches for years. That gap has made rare-disease diagnosis a flagship test case for medical AI, with papers regularly claiming that LLM pipelines outperform clinicians on benchmark case sets. But a recent meta-analysis warned that many of those evaluations carry a high risk of bias from suspected data leakage — the same problem that has undermined benchmarks across AI, from coding contests to math word problems. What was missing was a precise quantification of how much of the reported performance is real versus artifact. This study supplies that accounting, drawing on more than 60,000 cases from public repositories and independent clinical cohorts, and reconstructing a state-of-the-art agentic diagnostic framework to test it under controlled isolation.
key_points: Candidate-space contamination inflates agentic pipelines. When the team reconstructed a leading agentic diagnostic framework and allowed the usual one-vs-rest candidate setup, mean Recall@1 was 54.3%. Enforcing strict cross-dataset isolation — so the correct diagnosis could not already be present in the retrieval pool — dropped it to 40.3%, a large effect size (Hedges' g = 0.94).

Supervised classifiers show severe spatial overfitting. Models tuned and tested within the same cohort averaged 42.9% diagnostic accuracy, but when applied to external cohorts accuracy collapsed to 16.7% (Cohen's d = 2.01). The gap suggests models were learning cohort-specific shortcuts rather than transferable diagnostic signals.

Clinical narratives leak answers through treatment history. The audit shows LLMs often infer the correct diagnosis by spotting retrospective therapeutic cues — drugs or procedures mentioned in the case text that are only given after a diagnosis is known. This is hindsight pattern-matching, not differential reasoning from symptoms.

Knowledge-base timelines distort results. Temporal misalignment between when a model's foundational medical knowledge was frozen and when cases were recorded causes measurable performance swings, meaning some apparent gains or failures track database versioning rather than model capability.

The authors propose an evaluation framework. It couples strict data-isolation protocols with standardized benchmarking safeguards, aiming to make future rare-disease diagnostic AI report clinical robustness rather than leaderboard-friendly numbers.
report.impact: The implications reach across the medical AI stack. For the AI industry, it means headline benchmark numbers for clinical agents should be treated as unverified until isolation protocols are documented; vendors claiming diagnostic parity will face harder questions about their test design. For developers, the lesson is procedural: split candidates away from retrieval corpora, test on genuinely external cohorts, and audit for post-hoc cues like treatment mentions before celebrating accuracy. For patients and clinicians, the finding is a caution against early adoption — a model that scores well by recognizing leaked treatment history could fail precisely on the undiagnosed cases where help is needed most. The paper's framework also gives regulators and journals a concrete checklist for reviewing clinical AI claims.
report.tools: For follow-up, read the preprint directly (arXiv:2610.33592) and use Connected Papers or alphaXiv for related work on benchmark contamination. On the evaluation side, Inspect AI (UK AI Safety Institute) and Stanford's HELM/CrFM suites support reproducible, isolation-aware benchmarking. For data work, Hugging Face Datasets and PhysioNet/MIMIC-style repositories help construct strict train/test cohort splits. Pair these with knowledge bases such as OMIM or Orphanet to check temporal alignment between model knowledge cutoffs and case dates.
